title: Candlenut

names.note: 'The nuts are edible after roasting.' A second entry glosses bilar 'candlenut'.

identification.basis: The dictionary glosses bilar 'candle nut tree', and Roth (1901) gives billar as the Bloomfield River Koko-yellanji name of Aleurites moluccana. Anderson (1996) lists bilar, Aleurites moluccana, among the Bloomfield nut foods.

summary: **[Bilar](word:bilar)**, the candlenut (*Aleurites moluccanus*), is a rainforest tree with hard, round nuts that are 'edible after roasting' [ref:hershberger1982]. It was the most highly prized of the Bloomfield nuts: eaten on its own, and added to [wallaby](entry:wallaby) while it cooked for the flavour [ref:anderson1996]. The nut was roasted in a slow fire until it cracked [ref:roth1901]. Its oil fixed the [ochre](entry:red-ochre) on painted [spears](entry:spear-and-woomera) [ref:roth1904], its trunk was hollowed into outrigger [canoes](entry:canoes) [ref:anderson1996], and the big [grubs](entry:witchetty-grub) in candlenut wood were a favourite food [ref:anderson1996]. Raw, the nuts are strongly purgative [ref:rfk-aleurites].

infobox.label: Part used
infobox.value: Nuts (food, after roasting; oil for fixing ochre); trunk (dug-out canoes); grubs in the wood

infobox.label: Where
infobox.value: Rainforest, sea level to 800 m, mostly north of the Daintree River

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: The dictionary gives **[bilar](word:bilar)**: 'candle nut tree. The nuts are edible after roasting' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth's 1901 Bloomfield River list gives *billar* for *Aleurites moluccana* — the same word in his spelling [ref:roth1901]. At Cooktown, in Guugu Yimithirr country, he recorded *tarkal* [ref:roth1901]. Anderson also lists bilar, *Aleurites moluccana*, among the nut foods of Bloomfield [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Description
sections.body: A rainforest tree whose bark, on old trees, breaks into large plates. The leaves are 7–20 cm long and 4–13 cm wide, with one or two raised green or almost black glands on the upper side of the leaf stalk, and a covering of brown star-shaped hairs or scales underneath [ref:rfk-aleurites]. Young plants have deeply lobed leaves [ref:rfk-aleurites]. The flowers are small, 5–9 mm across. The fruit is round, about 4–6 cm across and usually two-lobed, and holds hard, round seeds about 2 cm across — the nuts. Rats commonly gnaw them [ref:rfk-aleurites].

sections.heading: Where it grows
sections.body: In Australia the candlenut grows in Cape York Peninsula and north-east Queensland, from near sea level to 800 m, 'mostly north of the Daintree River', with one isolated population on the central Queensland coast [ref:rfk-aleurites].

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
**Food.** Anderson calls the candlenut 'the most highly desired' of the Bloomfield nuts. It was roasted on the fire, needed no [leaching](entry:leaching), and was eaten on its own or added to [wallaby](entry:wallaby) carcasses to flavour them as they cooked [ref:anderson1996]. Like the other Bloomfield nuts it could be stored for up to two months, which helped in the [wet season](entry:seasons) [ref:anderson1996].

**Grubs.** The big [grubs](entry:witchetty-grub) that live in rotten or fallen candlenut trees were relished as food [ref:anderson1996].

**Oil for paint.** On the Bloomfield River the nut 'provides the "oil" used in fixing the [ochre](entry:red-ochre) for [spear](entry:spear-and-woomera)-painting' [ref:roth1904], and Anderson lists candlenut oil as the fixer for ochre [ref:anderson1996].

**Canoes.** Anderson names *Aleurites*, [red cedar](entry:red-cedar) and a cotton tree as the favourite timbers for the dug-out hull of Bloomfield outrigger canoes [ref:anderson1996]. The dictionary agrees, noting under *[wawuburra](word:wawuburra)* ([cotton tree](entry:cotton-tree)) that 'canoes were made out of these and the candlenut tree, bilar' [ref:hershberger1982].

**Elsewhere.** At Atherton (not Kuku Yalanji country), Roth watched a man score a sheet of [fig](entry:fig) bark for a [bark blanket](entry:bark-blankets) with the sharp edge of a broken candlenut shell [ref:roth1910-decoration].

sections.heading: How it was prepared
sections.body:
**Eating the nuts** [ref:roth1901] [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:anderson1996]:

1. **Gather** the fallen fruit: round, 4–6 cm across, each with one or two hard nuts inside [ref:rfk-aleurites].
2. **Roast** the fruit in a **slow fire**.
3. **When the nut cracks, it is fit to eat.** Break it open (the verb is *[dalkil](word:dalkil)*, 'to crack a nut') and eat the kernel.
4. No pounding, sifting or [leaching](entry:leaching) is needed for this nut [ref:anderson1996].

**Flavouring meat.** Add roasted candlenuts to a [wallaby](entry:wallaby) as it cooks [ref:anderson1996].

**Fixing paint.** The oily nut was used to fix [ochre](entry:red-ochre) on [spears](entry:spear-and-woomera) [ref:roth1904]. The sources do not describe how the oil was worked into the ochre. Kuku Yalanji words for the materials are *[wuba](word:wuba)* and *[murbuy](word:murbuy)* 'red ochre', *[makirr](word:makirr)* 'yellow ochre', and *[julngkal](word:julngkal)* 'to rub or paint on' [ref:hershberger1982].

**Canoes.** Bloomfield dug-outs were cut down with [stone axes](entry:stone), burnt out and scraped clean with adzes, and fitted with a single outrigger lashed on with [lawyer vine](entry:lawyer-cane) [ref:anderson1996]. The full method is under [red cedar](entry:red-cedar).

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body: 'The seeds of most species of *Aleurites* contain poisonous compounds', and candlenuts are 'strongly purging if eaten raw' [ref:rfk-aleurites]. The dictionary's rule is the one to follow: the nuts are edible *after roasting* [ref:hershberger1982]. Roast them until the shell cracks, as Roth describes [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body:
The candlenut is not listed as threatened; as a native plant it is 'least concern' wildlife under Queensland's Nature Conservation Act [ref:qld-plants-reg].

Native title holders' rights differ from place to place: see each place above. Under section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993*, native title holders do not need a licence or permit to hunt, fish or gather for their personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs [ref:alrc]. Everyone else needs the Traditional Owners' permission to take anything from country, and park rules apply.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: Related words: *[dalkil](word:dalkil)* 'to crack a nut'; *[munja-l](word:munja-l)* 'to gather, collect (e.g. nuts, plant food)'; *[wuba](word:wuba)* '[red ochre](entry:red-ochre)'; *[julngkal](word:julngkal)* 'to rub or paint on'; *[wawuburra](word:wawuburra)* 'cottontree', the other [canoe](entry:canoes) tree; and *[kaljan](word:kaljan)* 'outrigger canoe' [ref:hershberger1982].

locations.summary: **The candlenut does not grow on the Hann.** It is a rainforest tree, in Australia found 'mostly north of the Daintree River' [ref:rfk-aleurites], and the Hann runs through open woodland of 'stringybark, bloodwood, Moreton Bay ash and ironbark trees with a ground cover of coarse grasses such as speargrass' [ref:wp-hann]. The Atlas of Living Australia holds no candlenut record in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru [ref:ala-hann].

sections.heading: Where it grows here
sections.body: Not recorded. The nearest thing to rainforest in this country is downstream in Rinyirru, where the park's vegetation includes 'riverine closed forests' and 'vine thickets' among the woodlands and grasslands [ref:qpws-rinyirru-2013]; no candlenut is recorded there in the Atlas box either [ref:ala-hann].

sections.heading: How people used it here
sections.body: No published record was found of the Possum, Thaypan or Kuku Warra people using candlenut. The plant foods named for this country in the 2023 native title evidence are woodland foods: 'lady apples, white apples, bally yams that grow on a long stem, bush carrot and bush potato' [ref:fca-thaypan]. For how candlenut was eaten and used on the coast, see the general sections above.

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The upper Hann is the Possum People's country and the middle and lower Hann are Thaypan country, both recognised by the Federal Court in November 2023 [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan]. The Kuku Warra people, of the Laura side, hold a customary rights agreement with the Thaypan over the land between the North Kennedy and the Hann [ref:fca-kukuwarra].

locations.summary: Up on the Western Yalanji Mitchell the candlenut is not a tree of the river woodland: look for it only in the rainforest patches on the ranges [ref:ala-aleurites].

sections.heading: Where it grows here
sections.body: On **Western Yalanji** country it is a tree of the rainforest patches on the ranges, not the dry open woodland. One rainforest on the Mount Windsor Tableland, north of Mount Carbine, is even recorded by botanists as 'Candlenut Scrub' [ref:ala-aleurites].

locations.summary: Bilar is a tree of Eastern Kuku Yalanji country. In Australia it grows 'mostly north of the Daintree River' [ref:rfk-aleurites], and the Bloomfield records of eating the nuts, fixing ochre with the oil and hollowing the trunk into canoes all come from this coast [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Where it grows here
sections.body: That puts the heart of its Australian range on Eastern Kuku Yalanji country, in the rainforest between the Daintree and the Bloomfield. [ref:rfk-aleurites]

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: Much of Eastern Kuku Yalanji country is now Aboriginal land. On 29 September 2021 more than 160,000 ha, taking in the Daintree, Ngalba-bulal, Kalkajaka and Hope Islands national parks between Mossman and Cooktown, was handed back to the Eastern Kuku Yalanji people, to be jointly managed with the Queensland Government through the Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service [ref:ag2021].
